I've been going to a gym 3-4x a week for the last year and now that I have I have a drastically different understanding on how lazy and submissive fat people are. I always said when I had the money I would get a personal trainer - so I did. Was it a change? Yes, of course, but I made it part of my daily routine.

Do I enjoy the gym? Not at all. All the stuff I heard about "more energy, better well-being, you'll learn to love it" are crap. That may be true for most, and I highly suspect more applicable to fatties, but not me.

The gym is work, every time; however I know two things:
1. Going to the gym is good for my health.
2. If I don't do something I know is good for me out of laziness/apathy then I admit through living that I shouldn't try at difficult things.

Fatties don't want that. They want the world view to shift to benefit them. God forbid they lift a 5lbs dumbbell or walk for 10 min. If you know something is good for you why would you not do it?

I'm sorry you're not having an enjoyable experience. I used to hate it, then I learnt to love the gym, and I've never been fat.

I used positive reinforcement on myself to achieve this. I take a caffeine pill every time I go to the gym (it makes me feel energetic). I write it down on my task list every morning, so I feel rewarded when the time comes for me to cross it. And I use this app to remind me that building a habit requires time and hard work, but pays off nicely.

What has made it enjoyable for you? It's not that I do not see benefits, but my core reasoning is based on the fact of self-improvement. My body contours have changes, but I do not value them. My personal training is about to end and I know I will drift towards exercises I enjoy over others I do not and this may be a catalyst to my growth. Even with my trainer I go to the gym solo 1-2x/week. My greatest growth is commit to the gym lifestyle, even though I have done that already (if that makes sense).

Well, I learnt to appreciate the results. I always face it as a competition against my former self, so I feel excited to play against someone as devoted and as talented as myself. I take my glasses off (so I don't see anyone), I put on headphones with crappy uptempo pop songs (so I don't listen to anyone), and get lost in my own thoughts. In the end, it just got to me.

My personal training is about to end and I know I will drift towards exercises I enjoy over others I do not and this may be a catalyst to my growth.

Now, this is something that I don't do: focusing on exercises I don't like. I like benching, squatting, leg pressing, so I do these exercises a lot. I tolerate leg extensions, push ups, curls, so I do these exercises every other day. I hate crunches and lunges and I will never do them. But this happens to everyone, just find a program that works for you and follow it as closely as you can.

I have a love/hate relationship with squats.

It's the exercise I did most often, but I've never gained the flexibility to do it really well. I don't have the ankle flexibility to push my knees far enough forward. So to keep the weight balanced, I need to lean my torso much farther forward. This interferes with the actual lift, and I turn it into a good morning if I'm not careful.

Also, pushing myself to the edge of my flexibility is exhausting on its own. I havn't developed a daily stretching routine, but I probably stretch at least a bit every other day.
Isn't it getting easier each day, though? You should be improving quickly, especially at the beginning, if you just stick to the routine.

All the stuff I heard about "more energy, better well-being, you'll learn to love it" are crap.

Everyone I've heard who does some sort of cardio or lifting (gym or not) says how much energy they get right after. And then, there I am, wanting to practically sleep for weeks after I jog for 5 km or swim for an hour. I am completely drained for the rest of the day, even if I do that in the morning. The more often I do it, the more "dead" I am. Thus, there goes my motivation to keep on going every single time I try for a longer period of time.

I'm constantly yawning at the end of a session, I'm tired. I see that as different from body fatigue. There are days where my body is completely tapped out but I am without fatigue, but that is rare.

I always hear about people, doing a small activities and they feel great after - nope, I feel worse, but I know what I did was beneficial. I don't get an endorphin rush at all in strength or cardio. I am regular myself during these activities.

I go to the gym before work and I feel shitty for hours. My body is stronger, but it fucking hates working. Maybe I have a deep ingrained apathy I need to overcome to receive the "benefits", but I think they are mostly true only for fat people. It is easy to have more energy and feel better when you lose 25% of your excess fat - efficient heart, efficient lungs, a better integration of masses of flab. Fatties have it easier going to the gym as they reduced their life to nothingness.
